title: 19 Aug 2026
des: Saudi Prometric paediatrics recall, 19 August 2026 (test centre not stated)

questions.question: A term newborn has small pustules that rupture to leave collarettes of scale and hyperpigmented macules. What is the management?
questions.exp: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is benign; pustules are sterile and pigmented macules fade over weeks to months.

questions.question: A 2-day-old has blotchy erythematous macules with central yellow-white papules sparing the palms and soles. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema toxicum appears at 24-72 hours; smears show eosinophils; it resolves without treatment.

questions.question: A 3-year-old develops an unsteady wide-based gait 2 weeks after chickenpox. He is alert with no headache or vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia (classically after varicella) has a good prognosis and resolves over weeks.

questions.question: What is applied ethics?
questions.exp: Applied ethics deals with practical moral problems, such as clinical decisions; metaethics studies the nature of moral terms.
questions.a: The legal regulation of medical practice
questions.c: The branch of ethics that applies moral principles to real-life practical problems
questions.d: The study of the meaning of moral terms

questions.question: What is the main aim of a quality management strategy in health care?
questions.exp: Quality management aims at safe, effective care with prevention of risk and harm.
questions.a: To improve quality and safety and reduce harm to patients

questions.question: A child with a bone-anchored hearing aid (BAHA) has purulent discharge. A junior doctor prescribes antibiotics without a culture or senior advice, and the child later needs extra audiology assessment. Where is the main problem?
questions.exp: The error reflects a system and process failure: policies for culture and senior review were not followed.
questions.b: Failure to follow policies and systematic processes

questions.question: A child has deteriorating consciousness, very high transaminases, high ammonia, hypoglycaemia and prolonged clotting. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Encephalopathy with coagulopathy (INR > 1.5-2) and hypoglycaemia defines acute liver failure.

questions.question: A preterm infant on NG feeds deteriorates with increasing gastric residuals, abdominal distension and bloody stools. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: NEC: feed intolerance, distension and bloody stools in a preterm; X-ray may show pneumatosis intestinalis.

questions.question: A 3-week-old has sudden bilious vomiting and a soft abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

questions.question: An infant with suspected midgut volvulus is stable. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.exp: Upper GI contrast shows the abnormal duodenojejunal flexure or corkscrew; resuscitate, decompress with NG tube and involve surgeons urgently.

questions.question: A child treated for sinusitis with 10 days of amoxicillin now has persistent unilateral purulent nasal discharge with a foul smell. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Unilateral foul-smelling discharge in a young child suggests a retained nasal foreign body.

questions.question: A child has a nasal foreign body that cannot be removed in the emergency department. What is the next step?
questions.exp: ENT removal is needed when simple techniques fail; button batteries need urgent removal. The recall writer chose admission and ENT referral.
questions.d: Discharge and review in a week

questions.question: What is the mode of inheritance of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
questions.exp: DMD is X-linked recessive (dystrophin gene).

questions.question: A child is stung by a scorpion and has tachycardia, sweating and agitation. Which investigation is most useful?
questions.exp: Scorpion envenomation causes catecholamine surge with hyperglycaemia, leukocytosis and myocarditis; ECG and cardiac markers guide care. The recall writer chose CBC.
questions.b: CBC with glucose, electrolytes, ECG and troponin

questions.question: A child has constipation with soiling and impacted stool on rectal examination. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Diagnosis is clinical; X-ray is not routinely needed when impaction is felt on examination. The recall writer chose abdominal X-ray.

questions.question: A previously well, socially active 10-year-old develops new urinary incontinence. Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.exp: New-onset incontinence in a previously continent child needs exclusion of spinal cord pathology (tethered cord, tumour).

questions.question: A child has acute bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level and urinary retention a week after a viral illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A sensory level with sphincter involvement suggests a spinal cord lesion, such as transverse myelitis.

questions.question: A child admitted with dehydration after a viral illness becomes encephalopathic with multifocal neurological signs. Which investigation is best?
questions.exp: ADEM shows multifocal white matter lesions on MRI.

questions.question: Which type of pneumonia needs a follow-up chest X-ray?
questions.exp: Round pneumonia can mimic a mass, so repeat imaging is advised to confirm resolution.

questions.question: A child with lobar pneumonia from a gram-positive organism is unwell and admitted. What is the appropriate IV antibiotic?
questions.exp: Pneumococcus is the main gram-positive cause; IV ampicillin or ceftriaxone is used when oral treatment is not possible.

questions.question: A child has recurrent infections in the left lower lobe and a systemic arterial supply to a lung mass on CT angiography. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sequestration is non-functioning lung with systemic arterial supply, usually in the left lower lobe, with no bronchial communication.

questions.question: A child has a well-defined fluid-filled mediastinal cyst near the carina that does not communicate with the airway. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bronchogenic cysts are foregut duplication cysts, usually mediastinal or perihilar, without airway communication.

questions.question: A child with iron deficiency anaemia starts oral iron. Which parameter rises first?
questions.exp: Reticulocytosis appears within 3-5 days, peaking at 7-10 days; Hb rises over weeks.

questions.question: After a road traffic accident a child has bruising over the left chest, hypotension, tachycardia, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and normal equal breath sounds. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Beck triad with normal breath sounds suggests tamponade; tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds on one side.

questions.question: After a road traffic accident a child is tachycardic with cold peripheries, delayed capillary refill and BP 90/55. What is the state?
questions.exp: Normal BP with signs of poor perfusion is compensated shock; hypotension is a late sign in children.

questions.question: A child has swallowed a coin which is seen in the oesophagus on X-ray. What is the management?
questions.exp: Oesophageal coins should be removed endoscopically, urgently if symptomatic, or within 24 hours if not passing. The recall writer chose fluoroscopy with a magnet.

questions.question: An asymptomatic child has swallowed a coin which is now in the stomach on X-ray. What is the management?
questions.exp: Coins beyond the oesophagus usually pass; repeat X-ray if not passed in 2-4 weeks. Batteries and magnets differ.
questions.a: Reassure and observe for passage in stool

questions.question: A child who had an atrial switch for transposition years ago has bradycardia with dizzy spells. What is the most likely rhythm problem?
questions.exp: Atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) operations cause sinus node dysfunction.

questions.question: A child years after tetralogy of Fallot repair collapses and the ECG shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate management?
questions.exp: Repaired TOF carries risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death; VF needs unsynchronised defibrillation 4 J/kg.

questions.question: A 12-year-old has recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with nausea and photophobia, relieved by sleep, and a family history. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Migraine in children may be bilateral and shorter; family history and relief with sleep are typical.

questions.question: A child has stereotyped episodes of intense vomiting lasting days, separated by weeks of complete wellness. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cyclical vomiting is a migraine-equivalent with stereotyped episodes and normal health between them.

questions.question: A child has recurrent episodes of periumbilical pain with pallor and nausea lasting hours, normal between episodes, and a family history of migraine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Abdominal migraine is a functional disorder linked with migraine.

questions.question: A 3-year-old has fever for 6 days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fever ≥ 5 days plus 4 of 5 criteria; treat with IVIG and aspirin.

questions.question: A child has fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the hands and feet. What is the management?
questions.exp: HFMD (Coxsackie A16, enterovirus 71) is self-limiting; ensure hydration. The recall writer listed acyclovir and ceftriaxone as options.

questions.question: A 7-year-old is repeatedly angry, argues with adults, defies rules and deliberately annoys others, but does not harm people or animals. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: ODD lacks the serious rule violations and aggression of conduct disorder.

questions.question: A 6-year-old has taken money from his mother's purse. What is the best advice?
questions.exp: At this age, calm consistent consequences such as returning the item teach responsibility.
questions.a: Make him return the money and explain why it is wrong

questions.question: A 6-year-old still sucks his thumb. What is the advice?
questions.exp: Behavioural approaches come first; aversive taste agents are used if the child wants to stop. The recall writer chose aversion.
questions.d: Positive reinforcement and reminders; aversive bitter nail paint if needed

questions.question: What is the expected head circumference of a 6-month-old?
questions.exp: HC is about 35 cm at birth, about 44 cm at 6 months and about 47 cm at 1 year.

questions.question: A newborn at 1 minute has HR 80, irregular weak cry, some flexion, grimace and blue extremities. What is the Apgar score?
questions.exp: HR <100 = 1, weak cry = 1, some flexion = 1, grimace = 1, acrocyanosis = 1: total 5. The recall writer's keyed answer was 4 for a different scenario.

questions.question: A 20-kg child with severe haemophilia B needs a 50% factor IX rise for a joint bleed. What dose of factor IX is needed?
questions.exp: Factor IX: 1 IU/kg raises the level by about 1%, so dose = weight × desired rise = 20 × 50 = 1000 IU. Weight and target were reconstructed.

questions.question: A boy's father is 180 cm and his mother is 160 cm. What is his target (mid-parental) height range?
questions.exp: For boys: (father + mother + 13)/2 = 176.5 cm, with a range of ± 8.5 cm. The recall writer recorded 166-180 for parents not stated.

questions.question: A child in hospital is colonised with MRSA. Which precautions are needed?
questions.exp: MRSA requires contact precautions with gloves and gown.

questions.question: A child after bone marrow transplant is exposed to chickenpox. What should be given?
questions.exp: Non-immune immunocompromised patients need VZIG within 10 days of exposure (or acyclovir prophylaxis); live vaccine is contraindicated.

questions.question: A child on chemotherapy has a brother who has chickenpox. What should be done?
questions.exp: Non-immune children on chemotherapy need VZIG; oncology may delay chemotherapy if varicella develops. The recall writer chose stopping chemotherapy plus VZIG.
questions.a: Give VZIG (or post-exposure acyclovir) and seek oncology advice on chemotherapy

questions.question: An HIV-infected child recovering from Pneumocystis pneumonia is due vaccines. Which vaccines can be given?
questions.exp: Inactivated vaccines are safe; live vaccines are avoided in severely immunosuppressed children.
questions.a: Inactivated vaccines such as DTaP and pneumococcal

questions.question: A boy has declining school performance, behaviour change and adrenal insufficiency. Which investigation helps?
questions.exp: X-linked ALD: high VLCFA and posterior white matter changes on MRI brain.
questions.b: MRI brain and very long chain fatty acids

questions.question: A girl with normal early development now has regression, loss of hand use with hand-wringing and slowing head growth. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rett syndrome is caused by MECP2 mutations.

questions.question: A 6-month-old has clusters of sudden flexion spasms and developmental regression. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia on EEG; treat with ACTH, prednisolone or vigabatrin (tuberous sclerosis).

questions.question: A child who ingested a phenothiazine has drowsiness and miosis. Which other feature is typical?
questions.exp: Phenothiazines cause sedation, miosis, hypotension, extrapyramidal reactions and QT prolongation.

questions.question: A girl develops neck spasm and abnormal posturing after taking an antiemetic. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Metoclopramide causes acute dystonia; treat with diphenhydramine or benztropine.

questions.question: A student is found unresponsive in the school garden with slow breathing and pinpoint pupils. What is the management?
questions.exp: Opioid toxidrome: miosis, respiratory depression, coma. Give naloxone and support the airway.

questions.question: A neonate has haematuria, a palpable flank mass and thrombocytopenia. Which investigation is best?
questions.exp: Renal vein thrombosis classically follows dehydration, maternal diabetes or umbilical lines; Doppler confirms.

questions.question: A boy has learning disability, long face, large ears and macro-orchidism. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fragile X is diagnosed by PCR/Southern blot for FMR1 CGG repeats.
questions.a: DNA analysis for CGG repeat expansion in FMR1

questions.question: A child is diagnosed with coeliac disease. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet.

questions.question: A child with short bowel syndrome is starting enteral feeds. Which formula is preferred?
questions.exp: Elemental or hydrolysed formulas are better absorbed and reduce allergy risk in short gut.
questions.b: Amino acid-based or extensively hydrolysed formula

questions.question: A 13-year-old girl's height followed the 50th centile then plateaued at age 10, with breast development since age 8. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Early puberty causes an early growth spurt then early fusion and plateau. Details were reconstructed from a centile chart.
questions.b: Early puberty with early epiphyseal fusion

questions.question: A doctor is about to examine a crying child. What should he do first?
questions.exp: Hand hygiene comes before patient contact (WHO 5 moments).

questions.question: A doctor interrupts a nurse and gives orders without letting her speak. Which principle is involved?
questions.exp: Procedural justice concerns fair, respectful processes. Details of the scenario were limited.

questions.question: A doctor recommends a product made by a company he owns. What is this?
questions.exp: Financial interest in a recommendation must be declared or avoided.

questions.question: A research study is to be done in a hospital with an excellent reputation. What is most important?
questions.exp: Valid informed consent with disclosure of risks is the foundation of ethical research.

questions.question: A mother refuses MMR vaccine for her child. What should the doctor do?
questions.exp: Parental refusal of routine vaccines is managed by counselling and documentation. The recall writer chose telling the authority, which may apply under local mandatory vaccination rules.
questions.b: Explain the benefits and risks, address concerns and document the refusal

questions.question: A child shows signs of abuse by his father. What should the doctor do?
questions.exp: Suspected abuse must be reported to child protection services.
questions.a: Report to the child protection authority

questions.question: A febrile child has pain on neck flexion. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Meningism needs CSF examination unless contraindicated (raised ICP, instability, coagulopathy).

questions.question: A child with otitis media becomes irritable and has seizures. What is the next step after stabilisation?
questions.exp: Otitis media can spread to cause meningitis; CSF analysis is needed.
questions.c: Lumbar puncture (after imaging if focal signs)

questions.question: A 30-hour-old with transposition of the great arteries becomes cyanosed as the ductus closes. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.exp: PGE1 maintains ductal patency; balloon atrial septostomy if mixing remains inadequate.

questions.question: A child has failure to thrive, rickets, hyperchloraemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Normal anion gap hyperchloraemic acidosis with growth failure suggests RTA.

questions.question: A child has failure to thrive, recurrent chest infections, clubbing and a past admission for intussusception. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: CF can cause intussusception from thick inspissated stool.

questions.question: A child has fever for 5 days, joint pains, mild hepatosplenomegaly and a new apical murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Splenomegaly favours endocarditis; rheumatic fever usually does not cause splenomegaly. The recall writer was unsure between the two.

questions.question: A neonate has hyperammonaemia, metabolic acidosis with high anion gap, ketosis and hypoglycaemia. What is the likely group of disorders?
questions.exp: Organic acidaemias cause ketoacidosis with hyperammonaemia; urea cycle defects cause hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis.

questions.question: A 4-year-old who recently passed a worm in his stool swallowed a coin a day ago and now has intestinal obstruction. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Coins usually pass; a worm bolus is a known cause of obstruction. The recall writer was unsure.

questions.question: A preterm neonate with Rh alloimmunisation had an exchange transfusion via an umbilical vein catheter. After the transfusion he passes dark urine, with no oedema. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Dark urine after transfusion suggests haemoglobinuria from haemolysis. Details were reconstructed; the recall writer was unsure.

questions.question: A toilet-trained 3-year-old uncircumcised boy has suspected UTI. What is the best urine collection method?
questions.exp: Toilet-trained children can give a clean-catch sample, with retraction of the foreskin when possible.

questions.question: A 2-month-old has Hb 9.1 g/dL with normal MCV and is otherwise well. What is the management?
questions.exp: Physiological nadir at 8-12 weeks.

questions.question: Which clotting factors is cryoprecipitate rich in?
questions.exp: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF, FXIII and fibronectin.
questions.a: Factors II, VII, IX and X
questions.c: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII

questions.question: A girl has poor school performance, a webbed neck and short stature. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Turner syndrome (45,X) is confirmed by karyotype.

questions.question: A child with Williams syndrome has a murmur. Which cardiac lesion is typical?
questions.exp: Williams (7q11.23 elastin deletion): supravalvular AS, hypercalcaemia and elfin face.

questions.question: What is the typical length gain per month in the second 3 months of life?
questions.exp: About 3-3.5 cm/month in months 0-3, 2 cm/month in months 3-6, 1.5 cm/month in months 6-12.

questions.question: A 4-month-old's head circumference has grown from 35 cm at birth to 47 cm. Feeding is unchanged. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Rapid head growth suggests hydrocephalus; cranial ultrasound is ideal while the fontanelle is open.

questions.question: A child has mild dehydration from gastroenteritis. What is the management?
questions.exp: WHO plan A/B: ORS.

questions.question: After a road traffic accident a child has a tense tender abdomen and hip bruising and is still in shock after 3 crystalloid boluses. What is next?
questions.exp: Persistent shock after 40-60 mL/kg of fluid in trauma needs blood products and surgical control.

questions.question: What is the most common presenting feature of Hirschsprung disease?
questions.exp: Failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, then chronic constipation and distension.
questions.a: Delayed passage of meconium and constipation

questions.question: A preterm baby has a core temperature of 29 °C. Which finding is expected?
questions.exp: Severe hypothermia causes bradycardia, bradypnoea, hypoglycaemia and acidosis.

questions.question: A child has quotidian fever, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, arthritis and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: SJIA: daily fever spikes, salmon rash with fever, serositis and organomegaly.

questions.question: Which complication is typical of scleroderma (systemic sclerosis)?
questions.exp: Severe Raynaud phenomenon leads to digital ulceration, pitting and gangrene.
questions.d: Digital ulcers and gangrene from Raynaud phenomenon

questions.question: A child with proximal muscle weakness and a heliotrope rash is evaluated. Which test is most useful?
questions.exp: Muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase, LDH) are raised; MRI and biopsy support the diagnosis.

questions.question: A child had anaphylaxis after a vaccine. What is the next step before further vaccines?
questions.exp: Anaphylaxis to a dose contraindicates that vaccine; allergy evaluation identifies the component.
questions.a: Give the next dose as usual
questions.c: Give oral steroids before every vaccine
questions.d: Refer to an allergist for evaluation (skin testing for vaccine components)

questions.question: A 3-year-old cries and clings when her mother leaves her at nursery each morning, but settles after a few minutes. What is this?
questions.exp: Separation distress is normal in toddlers; a disorder is excessive, persistent and impairing.

questions.question: A child has culture-confirmed streptococcal pharyngitis. What is the duration of penicillin treatment?
questions.exp: 10 days of penicillin V or amoxicillin prevents rheumatic fever.

questions.question: A child has a swollen tender parotid with pus from Stensen's duct. What is the most useful investigation?
questions.exp: Bacterial (suppurative) parotitis is mostly Staphylococcus aureus; culture pus from the duct.

questions.question: An infant has congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type with massive proteinuria. Which medical treatment reduces the protein loss?
questions.exp: Steroid-resistant; ACE inhibitors and indomethacin reduce proteinuria, with albumin infusions.

questions.question: What is the definitive management of severe congenital nephrotic syndrome (Finnish type)?
questions.exp: Nephrectomy stops protein loss; dialysis bridges to transplant.
questions.c: Bilateral nephrectomy, dialysis, then renal transplant

questions.question: A preterm infant with low Apgar scores has low Hb, high urea and creatinine, hyperkalaemia and haematuria. What is the management?
questions.exp: Hypoxic AKI is managed supportively; peritoneal dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia or fluid overload. The recall writer chose peritoneal dialysis.
questions.c: Supportive care with fluid and potassium management, dialysis if refractory

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has a low Hb, a very low reticulocyte count, and normal white cells and platelets. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Parvovirus infects erythroid precursors, causing transient red cell aplasia.

questions.question: A child has short stature, skin hyperpigmentation, thumb anomalies and pancytopenia. Which investigation is diagnostic?
questions.exp: Fanconi anaemia is confirmed by increased chromosomal breakage; bone marrow shows hypocellularity. The recall writer chose bone marrow biopsy.

questions.question: A 10-year-old has signs of meningitis. What is the empirical antibiotic regimen?
questions.exp: Ceftriaxone with vancomycin for possible resistant pneumococcus.

questions.question: A child has a ring-enhancing lesion on CT after sinusitis. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Brain abscess needs cover for streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes.

questions.question: A toddler cries, holds his breath, turns blue and briefly goes limp, then recovers fully. What is the management?
questions.exp: Breath-holding spells are benign; iron supplements reduce them in iron deficiency.

questions.question: A young child has episodes of rhythmic thigh-rubbing with flushing and sweating, and is alert and can be distracted. What is the management?
questions.exp: Infantile masturbation (gratification) is benign and often mistaken for seizures.

questions.question: Which mechanism is involved in epileptogenesis?
questions.exp: Epileptogenesis involves ion channel changes (channelopathies) and altered synaptic transmission.

questions.question: During a mass vaccination campaign some people refuse. Which principle supports public health action?
questions.exp: In public health, protecting the community can justify measures limiting individual choice.
questions.d: Public interest may take precedence over individual preference

questions.question: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
questions.exp: Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, BCG, oral polio, rotavirus, yellow fever.

questions.question: Two units argue about a patient's care since admission. Which structured communication tool helps?
questions.exp: SBAR standardises handover between teams.

questions.question: A laboratory gives an urgent result by phone. What should the doctor do?
questions.exp: Read-back verification of critical results reduces errors.
questions.c: Read back and double-check identifiers and result

questions.question: A baby is born to a hepatitis B surface antigen-positive mother. What should be given?
questions.exp: Both vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours; breastfeeding is allowed.
questions.b: Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth

questions.question: A child is distressed after drinking gasoline. What is the most useful initial investigation?
questions.exp: Hydrocarbon aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis; assess oxygenation. Do not induce vomiting.
questions.a: Arterial blood gas and chest X-ray

questions.question: Which condition causes a false negative Mantoux test?
questions.exp: Malnutrition, immunosuppression, measles and recent live vaccines can blunt the response.

questions.question: Which condition causes a false negative sweat chloride test?
questions.exp: Oedema and hypoproteinaemia can lower sweat chloride; adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism cause false positives.

questions.question: A non-compliant asthmatic child presents with an exacerbation. What is the first treatment?
questions.exp: SABA is first-line for acute exacerbations; add steroids.

questions.question: A child with ALL in neutropenia has multiple hypoechoic lesions in the liver and spleen on ultrasound. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Chronic disseminated candidiasis gives bull's-eye lesions, often seen at neutrophil recovery.

questions.question: A child has rickets with normal calcium, high ALP, low phosphate and very high urinary phosphate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: XLH: FGF23 excess causes phosphate wasting with normal calcium and normal or low calcitriol.

questions.question: A short child has delayed bone age, normal growth velocity and a family history of late puberty. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Delayed bone age with normal velocity and family history; final height is normal.
questions.c: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.question: Which acid-base disturbance is typical in cystic fibrosis with salt loss?
questions.exp: Sweat salt loss causes hyponatraemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (pseudo-Bartter).
questions.a: Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap

questions.question: What is the antidote for organophosphate poisoning?
questions.exp: Atropine reverses muscarinic effects; pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase.

questions.question: How long should CPR usually continue in a child before considering stopping if there is no return of circulation?
questions.exp: There is no fixed limit; prolonged CPR is considered in hypothermia and drowning. The recall writer chose 20 minutes.
questions.d: About 20 minutes, guided by clinical context

questions.question: A child has ataxia, telangiectasia and recurrent infections. Which test supports the diagnosis?
questions.exp: AFP is raised in ataxia telangiectasia; IgA and IgG2 are often low.

questions.question: A child with febrile neutropenia has no identified source. Which organism must empirical antibiotics cover?
questions.exp: Empiric anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime). The recall item was "unconfirmed fever".

questions.question: A child has had bowel resection with an intact ileocaecal valve. Which complication is less likely than if the valve was removed?
questions.exp: Loss of the ileocaecal valve increases bacterial overgrowth and B12 malabsorption.

questions.question: A child has periumbilical pain moving to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, low-grade fever and rebound tenderness. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Migratory pain, anorexia and localised peritonism are classic.

questions.question: Which sign suggests a retrocaecal appendix?
questions.exp: Psoas sign suggests retrocaecal appendicitis; obturator sign suggests a pelvic appendix. The recall writer's options did not include psoas.

questions.question: Which finding is a major Duke criterion for infective endocarditis?
questions.exp: Major criteria: positive blood cultures with typical organisms and echocardiographic evidence.

questions.question: A child with cystic fibrosis has signs of pancreatitis. Which investigation is most helpful to confirm it?
questions.exp: Diagnosis needs 2 of: typical pain, lipase/amylase ≥ 3 × upper limit, imaging. CT is for complications. The recall writer chose CT.

questions.question: After liver transplantation a child has jaundice, raised transaminases and a very high GGT. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Disproportionately high GGT suggests biliary obstruction or cholangitis.

questions.question: A boy has precocious puberty with raised AFP and beta-hCG, and a brain mass on MRI. What is the tumour type?
questions.exp: hCG-secreting intracranial germ cell tumours cause precocious puberty in boys.

questions.question: Which condition is associated with optic nerve glioma (pilocytic astrocytoma)?
questions.exp: Optic pathway gliomas occur in about 15% of NF1.

questions.question: An infant has failure to thrive, hypotonia, coarse facies, a large tongue and an umbilical hernia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Prolonged jaundice, constipation, macroglossia, umbilical hernia and wide fontanelle.

questions.question: A newborn has a skin-covered sac protruding from the occiput. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Encephalocele is herniation of brain and meninges through a skull defect.

questions.question: A child with fever, neck stiffness and drooling has widened prevertebral soft tissue on lateral neck X-ray and is in airway distress. What is the immediate management?
questions.exp: Retropharyngeal abscess: airway protection, IV antibiotics and drainage. The recall writer chose nasotracheal intubation.
questions.b: Secure the airway in theatre and drain surgically with IV antibiotics

questions.question: An ill, toxic-looking child is drooling, sitting forward and has stridor. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keep calm, avoid examining the throat, secure the airway in theatre.

questions.question: A child with nephrotic syndrome has abdominal pain, fever and peritonitis. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: Pneumococcus causes spontaneous peritonitis in nephrotic syndrome.

questions.question: Which statement about sickle cell disease is correct?
questions.exp: Newborn screening allows penicillin prophylaxis and education, reducing mortality.
questions.a: HbF prevents all crises after infancy
questions.b: It can be diagnosed in the neonatal period by screening
questions.c: Early diagnosis does not change prognosis

questions.question: An infant becomes jaundiced with hepatomegaly, vomiting and hypoglycaemia after fruit and sweetened foods are introduced. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: HFI (aldolase B) presents at weaning with fructose or sucrose.

questions.question: After a road traffic accident a stable child has a seat-belt sign and fresh blood on rectal examination. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Seat-belt sign suggests hollow viscus and lumbar injury; contrast CT if stable.

questions.question: How are tics diagnosed?
questions.exp: Tics are a clinical diagnosis.

questions.question: A child's tics are worsening and impairing function. Which drug can be used?
questions.exp: Behavioural therapy first; alpha-agonists or antipsychotics for severe tics. The recall writer chose haloperidol.
questions.a: Clonidine, or an antipsychotic such as aripiprazole or haloperidol

questions.question: A fetus died from hydrops. Which test detects feto-maternal haemorrhage?
questions.exp: Kleihauer-Betke quantifies fetal cells in maternal blood.

questions.question: An infant with a 9-mm VSD has failure to thrive, a loud P2 and RV heave. What is the management?
questions.exp: Large VSD with heart failure and pulmonary hypertension needs early surgery to prevent Eisenmenger.
questions.d: Surgical closure (after catheter assessment of pulmonary vascular resistance if needed)

questions.question: Which cyanotic lesion causes oligaemic lung fields?
questions.exp: Reduced pulmonary flow: TOF, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia.

questions.question: An asthmatic child has more attacks in winter. What should the mother be advised?
questions.exp: Annual influenza vaccine reduces viral-triggered attacks.

questions.question: A boy injured while riding a bicycle develops trismus and generalised muscle spasms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Treat with TIG, metronidazole, wound care and muscle relaxants.

questions.question: A child has haematemesis, melaena and BP 55/30. What is the first step?
questions.exp: Resuscitation (ABC) comes first, then endoscopy.
questions.d: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid then blood

questions.question: A child has faecal impaction with overflow soiling. What is the first step?
questions.exp: Disimpaction then maintenance laxatives and toilet training.

questions.question: A child has progressive ataxia from age 2, oculocutaneous telangiectasia and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: ATM gene defect with immunodeficiency, cancer risk and raised AFP.

questions.question: A child has developmental delay and pica. What should be checked?
questions.exp: Pica increases lead exposure; lead causes cognitive impairment and anaemia.

questions.question: A 10-month-old sits without support but does not crawl or creep. He says mama and dada, waves bye-bye and has a mature pincer grasp. Which domain is delayed?
questions.exp: Pincer grasp, waving and babbling are normal at 10 months; most crawl by 9-10 months. Some children never crawl, so this is a mild concern.

questions.question: An infant has URTI symptoms then wheeze, tachypnoea and crackles, and family members have colds. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bronchiolitis (RSV) follows coryza in infants under 2 years.

questions.question: What proportion of serious adverse events involve communication failures?
questions.exp: Joint Commission data link communication failure to most sentinel events. The recall writer chose 80%.

questions.question: A child in pulseless VT receives a first shock without improvement. What energy should the second shock be?
questions.exp: PALS: 2 J/kg first, 4 J/kg second, up to 10 J/kg. The recall writer gave 60 J then 120 J.

questions.question: During infant BLS for a choking unconscious infant, two rescue breaths give no chest movement. What is next?
questions.exp: If breaths do not go in, reposition and retry, then start compressions.
questions.c: Reposition the airway and retry the breaths

questions.question: A toddler had a sudden choking episode with cyanosis that resolved, but now has reduced air entry on the right. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.question: An infant has hypotonia, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: SMA is confirmed by SMN1 deletion testing.
questions.b: Molecular genetic testing for SMN1 deletion

questions.question: What is the typical outcome of parasagittal watershed injury in term HIE?
questions.exp: Watershed injury affects proximal limbs (spastic quadriparesis); basal ganglia injury gives dyskinetic CP.

questions.question: An infant of a diabetic mother has respiratory distress and a high haematocrit. What is the mechanism of polycythaemia?
questions.exp: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia increases oxygen use, causing hypoxia and erythropoietin rise.
questions.b: Increased fetal erythropoiesis from chronic intrauterine hypoxia

questions.question: A preterm infant has respiratory distress soon after birth and a ground-glass chest X-ray with air bronchograms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Surfactant deficiency.

questions.question: A child on treatment for constipation has fever 38.9 °C, and urinalysis shows red cells and pus cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Constipation predisposes to UTI. Urine culture confirms.

questions.question: A febrile child has pyuria on urinalysis. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Culture is required to confirm UTI and guide antibiotics.

questions.question: Which sign accompanies a third cranial nerve palsy?
questions.exp: CN III palsy: ptosis, eye down and out, and dilated pupil (if compressive).

questions.question: A child with meningitis on ceftriaxone has a negative rapid Haemophilus test. What should be done?
questions.exp: Rapid antigen tests have false negatives; await cultures.
questions.a: Continue antibiotics until final culture results

questions.question: A febrile child with recent otitis media has been seizing for 20 minutes on arrival. There is no IV access yet. What is the first rescue medicine?
questions.exp: Benzodiazepine first, then a second-line agent.
questions.b: Benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam if access, otherwise buccal midazolam)

questions.question: A child has a severe generalised headache. What is the most important feature to look for?
questions.exp: Focal signs, papilloedema and altered consciousness suggest a secondary cause.

questions.question: A child has petechiae including on the palate, bruises of different ages, a recent URTI and platelets 25 × 10⁹/L. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: ITP follows viral infection; other counts are normal.

questions.question: A girl falls from a horse; GCS is 10, neck X-ray is normal but she cannot move her legs. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: SCIWORA: spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality; MRI shows cord injury.

questions.question: A child wakes 2-3 hours after sleep onset screaming and inconsolable, with no memory the next morning and no stereotyped movements. What is this?
questions.exp: Night terrors occur in non-REM sleep in the first third of the night with amnesia.

questions.question: A child has bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, seborrhoeic-like rash resistant to steroids and lytic skull lesions. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: LCH: punched-out skull lesions, rash, diabetes insipidus.

questions.question: An infant falls down stairs head-first, is fully conscious after the fall, then becomes drowsy hours later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: The lucid interval is classic for extradural haematoma.

questions.question: A child still seizing after 2 doses of benzodiazepine arrives in hospital. What is next?
questions.exp: After 2 benzodiazepine doses, give a second-line agent (levetiracetam, phenytoin, valproate).

questions.question: A child has refractory seizures, hypopigmented macules on the trunk and red papules on the face. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas.

questions.question: A febrile 1-year-old uncircumcised boy needs a urine sample. What is the best method?
questions.exp: Non-toilet-trained ill infants need a catheter or SPA sample.

questions.question: An obese child has not improved on diet restriction and has raised LDL. What is next?
questions.exp: Statins are considered from 8-10 years if LDL ≥ 190 or ≥ 160 with risk factors after lifestyle measures.
questions.a: Intensify lifestyle changes for 6 months; consider statins if LDL stays high

questions.question: A child has a decongestant overdose and narrow-complex HR 300/min. What is the treatment if stable?
questions.exp: SVT treatment: vagal manoeuvres then adenosine.

questions.question: A child has a pulse rate of 300/min. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: ECG distinguishes SVT from VT and sinus tachycardia.

questions.question: What is the most common type of choanal atresia on CT?
questions.exp: About 70% are mixed bony-membranous; 30% purely bony.

questions.question: An asthmatic child with infrequent attacks has just had a severe attack needing PICU. What is the preventer before discharge?
questions.exp: A life-threatening attack warrants daily controller treatment.

questions.question: A child with a history of asthma has sudden night-time barking cough and stridor without fever, which resolves quickly. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Spasmodic croup recurs at night, often with atopy.

questions.question: A child with a viral illness given two over-the-counter medicines develops vomiting, right upper quadrant pain and very high transaminases. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Multiple OTC products often contain paracetamol, causing unintentional overdose; give N-acetylcysteine.

questions.question: Parents of two sons with sickle cell disease ask about future pregnancies. What is the risk of an affected child?
questions.exp: Autosomal recessive: 25% affected, 50% carriers, each pregnancy.

questions.question: A child with allergic rhinitis using chronic nasal steroids has epistaxis. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Nasal steroids and allergic inflammation both irritate the mucosa. The recall writer chose allergic rhinitis.
questions.a: Nasal steroid use with mucosal irritation

questions.question: A child with 2 months of headache and unilateral green nasal discharge develops fever and periorbital swelling. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: CT distinguishes orbital from periorbital cellulitis and shows abscess.
questions.c: CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast

questions.question: A child walks upstairs with one hand held, runs, but cannot feed well with a spoon. What is the developmental age?
questions.exp: Runs and walks upstairs with hand held at 18 months; uses a spoon well at 18-24 months. The recall writer chose 2 years.

questions.question: A febrile 7-year-old was sent home well, but the blood culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae. On recall he is active with temperature 39 °C. What is the management?
questions.exp: Febrile children with positive cultures need re-assessment, repeat culture and antibiotics.
questions.d: Repeat blood culture and start antibiotics

questions.question: A child snores at night with witnessed apnoeas. What is the gold standard investigation?
questions.exp: Polysomnography is the gold standard.

questions.question: What is the first step in managing a child with appendicitis?
questions.exp: Resuscitation and antibiotics then appendicectomy.
questions.b: Admission with IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics

questions.question: A child bumped his head and felt dizzy for a few minutes but never lost consciousness and is now well. What is the management?
questions.exp: Low-risk head injury: discharge with safety-netting advice. The recall writer chose follow-up in 48 hours.

questions.question: A healthy term baby is ready for discharge. Which finding should prompt parents to return?
questions.exp: Recall options were incomplete; significant jaundice, poor feeding and fewer wet nappies are warning signs.
questions.a: Sleeping most of the day between feeds
questions.b: Jaundice spreading to the legs or appearing in the first 24 hours

questions.question: A 7-day-old has total bilirubin 147 µmol/L and direct 4.6 µmol/L, otherwise well. What type of jaundice is this?
questions.exp: Direct is a small fraction; mild unconjugated jaundice in a well baby at day 7 is usually physiological or breast milk related.

questions.question: What is the first-line antidepressant in children?
questions.exp: Fluoxetine has the best evidence in children.

questions.question: A teenage girl has disorganised speech and auditory and visual hallucinations, with a family history. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Psychosis lasting 6 months or more, with family history.

questions.question: A family was exposed to a house fire; carboxyhaemoglobin levels are all below 25%. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: High-flow oxygen shortens CO half-life; hyperbaric oxygen is for severe cases.
